learn.hook: In 1820 a teacher named Hans Christian Oersted noticed a compass needle twitch every time he switched on a current. Electricity was secretly making magnetism!
points: A wire carrying an electric current produces a magnetic field around it. This is the magnetic effect of current.
A compass needle placed near the wire deflects (turns) when the current flows and returns when the current stops.
If the direction of the current is reversed, the compass needle deflects in the opposite direction.
Winding the wire into a coil makes the magnetic effect stronger. A current-carrying coil behaves like a bar magnet with a north and a south pole.
Safety: do these activities only with dry cells and a switch, under adult supervision. Never use the electricity from wall sockets.

example.q: Think it through: Tara places a compass under a wire connected to a cell and a switch. The needle moves when she presses the switch. What happens if she swaps the cell's connections?
steps: The needle moves because the current makes a magnetic field.
Swapping the connections reverses the direction of the current.
A reversed current makes a reversed magnetic field.
example.answer: The needle will deflect in the opposite direction.

learn.reallife: Every electric motor in a ceiling fan, mixer-grinder or washing machine works because current-carrying coils behave like magnets.

games.title: Current and compass
items: A wire carrying current produces a magnetic field.

The magnetic field's direction depends on the direction of the current.
A current-carrying coil behaves like a bar magnet.
One end acts as a north pole and the other as a south pole.
It is safe to do this experiment with the wall socket.
Mains electricity is dangerous. Use only dry cells.

quiz.q: Who discovered that an electric current affects a compass needle?
quiz.explain: Oersted observed in 1820 that a current-carrying wire deflects a nearby compass needle.
steps: In 1820 Hans Christian Oersted saw a current-carrying wire deflect a compass needle
So he discovered the magnetic effect of current
Answer: Hans Christian Oersted
quiz.mistake: Does not know who discovered the magnetic effect of current

quiz.q: In which year did Oersted report the magnetic effect of current?
quiz.explain: Oersted's discovery was made and reported in 1820.
steps: Oersted made and reported his discovery
in the year 1820
Answer: 1820
quiz.mistake: Guesses the wrong century

quiz.q: A compass needle near a wire deflects only when the switch is ON. What does this show?
options: The wire is made of iron
A current produces a magnetic field
quiz.explain: The needle responds to the magnetic field that exists only while current flows.
steps: The needle moves only while current flows
So the current must produce a magnetic field
Answer: A current produces a magnetic field
quiz.mistake: Thinks the wire itself is magnetic even without current

quiz.q: What happens to the compass deflection if the current direction is reversed?
options: The needle deflects in the opposite direction
quiz.explain: Reversing the current reverses the magnetic field, so the needle turns the other way.
steps: The magnetic field's direction depends on the current's direction
Reversing the current reverses the field, so the needle deflects the opposite way
Answer: The needle deflects in the opposite direction
quiz.mistake: Thinks the field does not depend on current direction

quiz.q: Why is a coil better than a straight wire for showing the magnetic effect?
options: A coil makes the magnetic effect stronger
A coil makes the current disappear
quiz.explain: In a coil, the magnetic fields of all the turns add up, giving a stronger effect.
steps: In a coil, the magnetic fields of all the turns add up
So a coil makes the magnetic effect stronger than a straight wire
Answer: A coil makes the magnetic effect stronger
quiz.mistake: Does not know that turns add up their magnetic effect

quiz.q: A current-carrying coil behaves most like:
quiz.explain: It has a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other, like a bar magnet.
steps: A current-carrying coil has a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other
So it behaves like a bar magnet
Answer: A bar magnet
quiz.mistake: Does not connect a coil's field with a bar magnet's

quiz.q: Which household appliance uses the magnetic effect of current in its motor?
options: Pressure cooker on a gas stove
quiz.explain: The fan's electric motor uses current-carrying coils that act like magnets to make it spin.
steps: An electric motor uses current-carrying coils that act like magnets
A ceiling fan runs on such a motor
Answer: Ceiling fan
quiz.mistake: Does not know that motors depend on the magnetic effect

quiz.q: What is the safest power source for a school compass-and-wire experiment?
options: A dry cell with a switch
quiz.explain: Dry cells give a small, safe current. Mains electricity can give a dangerous shock.
steps: Dry cells give only a small current
With a switch they are safe for school experiments; mains electricity can give a dangerous shock
Answer: A dry cell with a switch
quiz.mistake: Does not realise mains electricity is dangerous

teach.ask: Gappu stares at a compass: Why does this needle jump when you switch on the wire's current?
teach.praise: So a current makes a magnetic field and that pushes the compass needle. Electricity and magnets are friends!
teach.nudge: What does the current in the wire produce around it? And what does that do to the needle?

revise.summary: A wire carrying current produces a magnetic field around it, so a nearby compass needle deflects; reversing the current reverses the deflection (Oersted, 1820). Winding the wire into a coil makes the effect stronger, and the coil behaves like a bar magnet.
focus: Observing the magnetic effect with a compass
Why a coil is stronger, and coil as a bar magnet
remember: Oersted discovered the magnetic effect of current in 1820
Reversing the current reverses the compass deflection
A current-carrying coil acts like a bar magnet with north and south poles
traps: The needle moves only while the current flows, not because the wire is iron
Never use wall sockets for these experiments — use dry cells and a switch

learn.hook: A giant crane in a scrapyard lifts a whole car with a magnet, then drops it with the flick of a switch. That is an electromagnet at work!
points: An electromagnet is a coil of insulated wire wound around a soft iron core (like an iron nail). It is a magnet only while current flows.
It becomes stronger with more turns of wire, a larger current (for example, more cells), and an iron core inside the coil.
Reversing the current reverses its north and south poles.
Unlike a permanent magnet, an electromagnet can be switched on and off, and its strength can be changed.
Uses: cranes that lift iron scrap, electric bells, loudspeakers, electric motors and machines that separate iron from waste.

example.q: Think it through: Dev's nail electromagnet picks up 4 pins. He wants it to pick up more pins. Suggest two changes.
steps: Strength depends on the number of turns of wire.
Strength also depends on the size of the current.
So add turns, or use more cells in series (with adult supervision).
example.answer: Wind more turns of wire around the nail, or increase the current by adding another cell.

learn.reallife: In an electric bell, an electromagnet pulls a metal strip that makes the hammer hit the gong, again and again, very fast. Trrring!

quiz.q: What is an electromagnet made of?
options: A coil of insulated wire around an iron core
A plastic rod rubbed with silk
A glass lens and a mirror
A wooden stick and a string
quiz.explain: Current through the coil magnetises the iron core.
steps: An electromagnet is a coil of insulated wire around a soft iron core
Current through the coil magnetises the core
Answer: A coil of insulated wire around an iron core
quiz.mistake: Does not know the parts of an electromagnet

quiz.q: When does an electromagnet act as a magnet?
options: Only while current flows through its coil
quiz.explain: Switch off the current and the soft iron core loses most of its magnetism.
steps: The iron core is magnetised only by the current
So it acts as a magnet only while current flows through its coil
Answer: Only while current flows through its coil
quiz.mistake: Thinks an electromagnet is a permanent magnet

quiz.q: Which change will make an electromagnet stronger?
quiz.explain: More turns add up their magnetic effects, making a stronger magnet.
steps: Strength increases with more turns, a larger current and an iron core
So increasing the number of turns makes it stronger
Answer: Increasing the number of turns
quiz.mistake: Thinks fewer turns or a non-magnetic core make it stronger

quiz.q: Why does a scrapyard use an electromagnet instead of a permanent magnet?
options: It can be switched off to drop the scrap
quiz.explain: Switching off the current releases the load, which a permanent magnet cannot do.
steps: An electromagnet can be switched off
Switching off releases the scrap, which a permanent magnet cannot do
Answer: It can be switched off to drop the scrap
quiz.mistake: Misses the main advantage of an electromagnet

quiz.q: How can you reverse the poles of an electromagnet?
options: Reverse the direction of the current
quiz.explain: The poles depend on the current's direction, so reversing the current swaps them.
steps: The poles depend on the direction of the current
Reversing the current swaps north and south
Answer: Reverse the direction of the current
quiz.mistake: Does not link pole direction with current direction

quiz.q: Which of these uses an electromagnet?
quiz.explain: In an electric bell, an electromagnet repeatedly pulls a metal strip to ring the gong.
steps: In an electric bell, an electromagnet repeatedly pulls a metal strip
This makes the hammer strike the gong
Answer: Electric bell
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise everyday devices with electromagnets

quiz.q: Which material is best for the core of an electromagnet?
quiz.explain: Soft iron becomes strongly magnetic while current flows and loses its magnetism quickly when switched off.
steps: Soft iron becomes strongly magnetic while current flows
It loses its magnetism quickly when switched off, so it is the best core
Answer: Soft iron
quiz.mistake: Thinks any material can be a good core

quiz.q: Why must the wire in an electromagnet be insulated?
options: So current flows around every turn instead of jumping across touching turns
To stop it from being magnetic
quiz.explain: If bare turns touched, current would take a short path and the coil would not work properly.
steps: If bare turns touched, current would take a short path across them
Insulation keeps the current flowing through every turn
Answer: So current flows around every turn instead of jumping across touching turns
quiz.mistake: Does not know why insulation is needed in a coil

teach.ask: Gappu tries to lift a pin with a nail: Nothing happens! How do I turn this nail into a magnet that I can switch off?
teach.praise: Wrap wire around the iron nail, send current, and it becomes a magnet. Switch off and it lets go. Magic!
teach.nudge: What should I wrap around the nail? And what has to flow through it?

revise.summary: An electromagnet is a coil of insulated wire around a soft iron core that is a magnet only while current flows. It gets stronger with more turns, more current and an iron core; reversing the current reverses its poles, and it can be switched on and off.
focus: Parts of an electromagnet and when it works
Uses: cranes, electric bells, loudspeakers, motors
remember: Electromagnet = insulated coil around a soft iron core; a magnet only while current flows
Stronger with more turns, larger current, iron core
Uses: scrap cranes, electric bells, loudspeakers, electric motors
traps: Fewer turns or a plastic core make it weaker, not stronger
Bare wire won't do — the coil must be insulated

learn.hook: Why does an old-style bulb get too hot to touch while an LED stays cool? It is all about the heating effect of current!
points: When current flows through a wire, the wire gets heated. This is the heating effect of electric current.
The heat produced depends on the material, length and thickness of the wire and on the size of the current.
Heaters, electric irons, toasters, kettles and immersion rods use a coil of nichrome alloy, which gets very hot without melting.
In a filament bulb, a thin tungsten filament glows white-hot, but most of the energy is lost as heat. LEDs give the same light using much less electricity.
A fuse is a safety device with a wire of low melting point. If too much current flows, the wire melts and breaks the circuit. Today many homes use MCBs, which switch off automatically.

example.q: Think it through: Too many appliances are plugged into one extension board and the fuse in the house 'blows'. Was the fuse faulty?
steps: Many appliances together draw a large current.
A large current heats the fuse wire strongly.
The fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit before the house wiring overheats.
example.answer: No. The fuse worked correctly and protected the wiring from overheating and possible fire.

learn.reallife: Electrical appliances in India carry the ISI or BIS mark to show they meet safety standards. Always ask an adult or an electrician to replace a fuse.

quiz.q: Which appliance works mainly on the heating effect of current?
quiz.explain: An electric iron has a heating element that gets hot when current flows.
steps: An electric iron has a heating element
It gets hot when current flows, so it works on the heating effect
Answer: Electric iron
quiz.mistake: Mixes up appliances using heating and magnetic effects

quiz.q: What is the job of a fuse in a circuit?
options: To melt and break the circuit when the current is too large
quiz.explain: A fuse protects wiring and appliances by cutting the circuit when too much current flows.
steps: A fuse wire melts when too much current flows
This breaks the circuit and protects the wiring and appliances
Answer: To melt and break the circuit when the current is too large
quiz.mistake: Thinks a fuse helps or stores current

quiz.q: Why is a fuse wire made of a material with a low melting point?
options: So it melts quickly when the current is too large
quiz.explain: It must melt before the house wiring gets dangerously hot.
steps: The fuse must melt before the house wiring gets dangerously hot
So it is made of a material with a low melting point
Answer: So it melts quickly when the current is too large
quiz.mistake: Does not link melting point with the purpose of a fuse

quiz.q: Which material is commonly used for the heating element of a room heater?
quiz.explain: Nichrome gets very hot when current flows but does not melt or burn easily.
steps: The heating element must get very hot without melting or burning
Nichrome alloy does this, so heaters use nichrome
Answer: Nichrome
quiz.mistake: Thinks good conducting wires like copper are used as heating elements

quiz.q: Why do LED bulbs save electricity compared with filament bulbs?
options: They waste much less energy as heat
They glow only in the dark
quiz.explain: A filament bulb turns most of its energy into heat. An LED turns much more into light.
steps: A filament bulb turns most of its energy into heat
An LED turns much more into light, so it uses less electricity
Answer: They waste much less energy as heat
quiz.mistake: Does not realise filament bulbs waste energy as heat

quiz.q: The filament of an old-style bulb is made of:
quiz.explain: Tungsten has a very high melting point, so it can glow white-hot without melting.
steps: A filament must glow white-hot without melting
Tungsten has a very high melting point, so it is used
Answer: Tungsten
quiz.mistake: Confuses the filament material with heater wire

quiz.q: What does an MCB do?
options: Switches off the circuit automatically when the current is too large
quiz.explain: An MCB (miniature circuit breaker) does the job of a fuse and can be switched back on after the fault is fixed.
steps: An MCB (miniature circuit breaker) does the job of a fuse
It switches off automatically when the current is too large and can be switched back on
Answer: Switches off the circuit automatically when the current is too large
quiz.mistake: Does not know MCBs are safety switches

quiz.q: Which is a safe habit with electric heating appliances?
options: Plugging many heaters into one socket
Switching off and unplugging the iron after use
Touching the heating coil to test it
quiz.explain: Unplugging after use prevents overheating and accidents. The other actions are dangerous.
steps: Unplugging the iron after use prevents overheating and accidents
Many heaters on one socket, touching coils or wet hands are dangerous
Answer: Switching off and unplugging the iron after use
quiz.mistake: Does not recognise unsafe electrical habits

teach.ask: Gappu warms his wings near a heater: How does electricity make this coil so hot? And why do houses have fuses?
teach.praise: Current heats the wire, and a fuse melts to break the circuit if too much current flows. Hot and safe!
teach.nudge: What happens to a wire when current flows? And what does a fuse do when there is too much current?

revise.summary: Current flowing through a wire heats it (heating effect). Heaters and irons use nichrome coils, filament bulbs use tungsten (but waste energy as heat, unlike LEDs), and a fuse or MCB breaks the circuit when too much current flows.
focus: Appliances that use the heating effect
How a fuse and an MCB protect a circuit
Materials: nichrome (heating element), tungsten (filament), low-melting fuse wire
LED versus filament bulb and safe habits
remember: Heating elements: nichrome; bulb filament: tungsten
Fuse: low-melting wire that melts when current is too large; MCB switches off automatically
LEDs waste much less energy as heat than filament bulbs
traps: A blown fuse usually means it did its job, not that it was faulty
A fuse wire must have a low, not high, melting point
An electric bell works on the magnetic, not heating, effect
